study.title: Light and Sound Design
study.question: How do lighting and sound tell the story?
study.passage:
Design basics (written for this lesson):
Lighting: Colour (warm amber = comfort, morning, home; cool blue = night, sadness, cold; red = danger or anger; green = eerie). Intensity (bright = energy, dim = quiet or mystery). Direction (front light shows faces; backlight creates silhouettes; side light creates drama). Timing (snap = sudden, fade = gradual).
Sound: Effects (doorbell, rain, traffic), music (sets mood), silence (creates tension), volume and fades.
Cue sheet format: Cue number | Type (LX or SFX) | Trigger (line or action) | Description | Timing. Example: LX 1 | Lights | Pre-show to start | Slow fade up to warm wash | 5 s. SFX 1 | Sound | After "Where is everyone?" | Distant thunder | 3 s fade in.
Task: Design 4–6 lighting and sound cues for your group play. Write a cue sheet and explain the mood each creates. If the school has stage lights, test them; if not, use desk lamps, phone flashlights with coloured cellophane and a speaker.

study.title: Design the Space
study.question: How does a set tell the audience where they are and how to feel?
study.passage:
Set design task (written for this lesson):
1. Compare (10 minutes): Look at photos of a realistic set (a detailed kitchen) and a minimalist set (a single door frame on an empty stage). What does each communicate? What does each cost in time and money?
2. Analyze your play (10 minutes): For each scene, list where and when it happens and the mood.
3. Design (20 minutes): Create a set for your group play using only items available at school (chairs, tables, boxes, fabric, a ladder, cardboard). Requirements: suits every scene or changes quickly; leaves room to move; keeps clear sightlines; includes at least one symbolic set piece (for example, a single empty chair for a missing person).
4. Draw: a ground plan (from above, with the audience at the bottom, stage areas marked and furniture as labelled shapes) and a front-view sketch with colour notes.
5. Explain: one paragraph on how your set supports the play's mood and theme.

body.objective: Students will be able to write a theatre review.
body.iCan: I can write a theatre review.
successCriteria: I can describe a performance accurately
I can analyze acting, directing and design using drama vocabulary
I can write a balanced theatre review with evidence
body.hook: Theatre critics can help a show sell out or close early. A good review doesn't just say "loved it" or "hated it." It describes what happened, analyzes how it worked, and gives a reasoned judgement that helps readers decide.

vocabulary.definition: A written evaluation of a performance.
Including both strengths and areas for improvement.
Specific moments from the performance that support a judgement.
Acting, directing, set, lighting, sound, costumes and props.

study.title: Write Like a Critic
study.question: How do I write a fair, convincing theatre review?
study.passage:
Review structure (written for this lesson):
1. Introduction: title of the play, who performed it, when and where, and a one-sentence overall judgement.
2. Summary: a short description of the story without giving away the ending.
3. Acting: one or two performers; use specific moments and drama vocabulary (projection, physicality, subtext, focus, commitment).
4. Directing and design: comment on blocking, transitions, lighting, sound, set and costumes.
5. Conclusion: overall evaluation and who would enjoy it.
Evidence example (written for this lesson): Weak: "The acting was good." Strong: "When Jordan finally whispered 'What if I'm not good enough?' after a long pause, the room went silent; the slow pace made the confession feel real."
Task: Watch a classmate group's play (or a recorded school production) and write a 300-word review. Be respectful: criticize choices, not people.
